filter syntax, and patch operations

Here is a fact that should alarm anyone
who runs a security program. A 2023
Verizon data breach investigations
report analysis found that orphaned
accounts valid credentials belonging to
people who no longer work at a company
are one of the most reliably exploited
initial access vectors in enterprise
breaches. Not because attackers are
sophisticated because IT teams are
overwhelmed. Someone leaves on a Friday
afternoon, their manager forgets to file
the ticket and that Salesforce login
stays live for weeks. Multiply that
across Slack, GitHub, Zoom, Jira,
Confluence, and every other SAS tool the
company subscribes to, and you have an
enormous, perpetually growing attack
surface. Today's concept is SEIM,
pronounced SKIM, the system for
cross-domain identity management. SECIM
is the open standard that replaces
manual provisioning with a real-time
automated protocol. When your HR system
records a new hire, SCIM creates the
accounts. When someone moves teams, SCIM
updates the permissions. When someone is
terminated, SCIM disables access in
seconds, not days.
Think of SEIM like a postal address
standard. Before postal codes existed,
every country, every city, every courier
had its own addressing convention.
Sending a letter internationally
required knowing the local format for
each country, which meant custom
knowledge, custom handling, and lots of
things getting lost. Postal codes
standardize the format so that any
sender anywhere in the world could
address a letter to any recipient and
any postal system could process it
without custom translation. SCIM does
the same thing for identity. Before
SCIM, every IDP, Octa, Azure, Active
Directory, Ping, identity, workday had
to build custom connectors for every SAS
application, Salesforce, Slack, GitHub,
Service. Now, each connector used that
app's proprietary API. When the app
updated its API, the connector broke.
When a new SAS tool arrived, someone had
to build another connector from scratch.
SCIM replaces all of that with a single
standard REST API. Any IDP that speaks
SECIM can provision any SAS app that
implements SCIM. No custom connector, no
fragile bespoke integration, no
connector maintenance backlog.
Let me give you a concrete picture of
what life without SCIM looks like in a
mid-sized company. It is Monday morning
and a new software engineer is starting.
The HR team inputs her details into
workday that triggers a Jira ticket to
it. It must now manually create accounts
in Octa for SSO, GitHub Enterprise for
source code access, Slack for team
communication, Google Workspace for
email, Zoom for video calls, Jira and
Confluence for project management, and
data dog for monitoring access. And that
is before counting the halfozen internal
tools. Each of those has a different
admin interface, a different permission
model, and a different definition of
what a group membership means. The
average Fortune 500 company uses over
200 SAS applications. If each one
requires a manually created account, new
hire onboarding takes hours to days.
When someone moves from the engineering
team to the platform team, those group
memberships must be updated everywhere
and they almost never are consistently.
When someone leaves the provisioning
ticket competes with everything else in
the ITQ, the result is orphaned
accounts, stale permissions, and a
compliance nightmare every time an
auditor asks to confirm that no former
employees have active access. SEIM
defines a standardized client server
model. The SEIM client, typically your
IDP, is the party that pushes changes.
The SEIM server is the SAS application
that implements the API. The client
detects identity changes from its
authoritative source, HR, and platform,
a directory, and translates them into
standard HTTP operations against the
servers resource endpoints.
SCIM is actually three RFC's published
together in September 2015. RFC 7642
defines the concepts and terminology.
RFC 7643 defines the core schema, the
JSo data model for users and groups. RFC
7644 defines the protocol, the HTTP API.
The two core resource types are user and
group. A user resource has a rich set of
standardized attributes. Username name
with given name and family name. Emails
as an array of typed values. phone
numbers, a title field, a department, a
manager reference, and critically the
active boolean which controls whether
the account is enabled or disabled.
Beyond the core attributes, SCIM has an
extension model. The enterprise user
extension identified by a earn uniform
resource name adds attributes like
employee number, cost center,
organization, and manager. Custom
extensions follow the same pattern.
Resources are accessed through a
predictable URL structure. Users live at
SL users. Groups live at SLGroups.
Individual resources are at SL users/
their unique identifier. SCIM also
exposes three discovery endpoints.
SLService provider config tells the
client which optional features the
server supports including bulk
operations, filtering, sorting, e tags,
patch, and password management. SLS
scheas lists every attribute in every
schema the server supports. SL resource
types lists which resource types are
available. The SCIM client begins by
consulting service provider config to
know what the server is capable of, then
proceeds with provisioning operations
using only the features the server has
declared support for.
Let me walk you through the four
operations you will encounter in a real
SCIM integration. Creating a user is a
post to SL users with a JSo body that
includes a schemas array declaring which
extensions are in use. Then the standard
attributes username, name, emails,
title, active set to true and any
enterprise extension attributes like
department and manager. The server
responds with 201 created and returns
the full resource including its server
signed id and a metab block containing
the resource location and an e tag
version string. Updating a user uses
HTTP patch notput. SCIM defines three
patch operation types add, remove, and
replace. Each operation has an optional
path expression that can target a
specific attribute or even a specific
array element using a filter. For
example, to update just the title
attribute, you send a patch with op
equals replace path equals title and the
new value. To remove a specific group
member without rewriting the entire
member's array, you send a remove
operation with a path filter targeting
that member. Deprovisioning is another
patch operation setting active to false.
This is the preferred approach over
delete because it is reversible. If the
termination is reversed, the account can
simply be reenabled. A hard delete is
permanent by spec. There is no soft
delete. For large-scale onboarding or
reconciliation jobs, the bulk endpoint
lets you bundle many operations into a
single HTTP request with cross
references using bulkhead. So you can
create a user and add them to a group in
the same request.
SCIM service accounts deserve the same
threat modeling attention as any other
privileged infrastructure credential.
The most destructive attack is
unauthorized bulk deletion. A SCIM
service account that has delete access
and is compromised can disable or
permanently delete every user account in
a target application in a single bulk
request. The impact is a complete denial
of service for every user. Mitigation
requires restricting service accounts to
the minimum necessary operations. In
most deployments, that means create,
read, and patch, but never delete in
production. combined with rate limiting
and anomaly detection on bulk calls. The
second major risk is stale account
harvesting. When a SCIM connector fails
silently, a token expired, a network
partition, a misconfigured retry policy,
accounts that should have been to
provisioned remain active. Former
employees can log in or the accounts can
be targeted for credential stuffing.
Mitigation requires monitoring connector
sync lag and alerting when accounts are
active in a SAS tool but marked inactive
in the IDP. The third risk is the
overprivileged service account. SEIM
tokens are often long-ived bearer tokens
with admin level scope. An attacker who
obtains this token can enumerate the
entire user directory, read all employee
attributes, including personally
identifiable information, and create new
privileged accounts. Service accounts
should be scoped to specific resource
types and specific operations, bound to
source IP or mutual TLS where possible,
and stored in a secrets manager rather
than hard-coded in configuration. A
final risk is endpoint enumeration. The
discovery endpoints are often accessible
without authentication, revealing the
servers capabilities and providing
valuable reconnaissance for a targeted
attacker.
SEIM2 has been the enterprise
provisioning standard for a decade and
its adoption has accelerated
considerably in recent years. Every
major IDP, Octa, Microsoft Entra ID,
Google Ping, Forgro ships SEIM2
connectors and procurement teams at
large enterprises now require SEIM
support as a condition for SAS vendor
approval. The IETF SEIM working group is
actively developing SCIM3 tracked as
draftf API v3. The focus is not on
reinventing the protocol, but on
tightening the parts where
interoperability testing revealed
ambiguity, particularly patch path
expression semantics, the error response
format and the discovery documents.
Importantly, SCIM3 will not break the
wire format for existing two
deployments. So, migrations should be
non-disruptive. The more transformative
work is the SCIM event specification,
draftfim events. SCIM2 is fundamentally
a push protocol. The IDP pushes changes
to the service provider, but there is no
standardized way for the service
provider to notify the IDP of changes
that happen locally, like a user being
suspended in the app itself. SCIM events
fixes this by adapting the security
event token framework, the same set
format used by the shared signals
framework and CAP to carry SCIM change
notifications as asynchronous push
events. This closes the long-standing
one-way sync gap and reduces reliance on
polling reconciliation jobs. Combined
with the zero trust architectural
principle of continuous validation, the
trajectory is clear. SCIM will become
the foundation for realtime birectional
identity life cycle management across
the enterprise stack.
